articles.title: Chainalysis Breach Exposes Global Law Enforcement Crypto Surveillance
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It’s unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you… Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.” In a Wednesday update, the company said that part of the “ongoing multifront cyberattack” involved an “on-path attack” that exposed a subset of customer passwords, and that the attack vector had been identified and fixed. Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties. Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted. The company said later that day that an investigation two days earlier (on Monday) had revealed that “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.” It also said it had detected “abnormal activity” and, in response, took down its login page and know-your-transaction service, which monitors threats to cryptocurrency holdings in real time. The company has also removed access to its Reactor and Data Solutions services. In an update on Friday, Chainalysis said it had begun phasing in customer access to KYT and Address Screening and expected more customers to follow. It asked customers to submit their trusted IP addresses so they can be added to an allow list and to prepare to reset credentials once they regain access. The credential rotation is mandatory. The company says its investigation has yet to reveal any evidence that any investigation data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated. Several important questions remain unanswered. As noted, the source that made the on-path attack possible is still unknown. It’s not clear how useful the information obtained in such an attack would be unless the attackers also had the ability to decrypt the traffic they were monitoring. If that were the case, the attackers might have gained broad control of the company’s infrastructure. Chainalysis also didn’t explain why it waited until Wednesday to disclose the data theft of all customers’ personal information when its investigation discovered the exposure two days earlier. Further, the company has provided no details about the AI agents used in the attack and how they worked. A Chainalysis representative said the company wasn’t commenting beyond the statements in its blog post. articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source The government yesterday authorized the activation of its NT$500 billion (US$15.26 billion) National Stabilization Fund (NSF) to support local shares, as the stock market experienced significant fluctuations while uncertainties in the international political and economic situation continue. The NSF’s steering committee may use the fund to intervene in the market to prop up local shares, the Ministry of Finance said in a statement. Once the fund is activated next week, it would be the 10th time the NSF has intervened in the market. Separately, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) yesterday announced temporary curbs on short selling shares and other measures to help maintain stock market stability, with the rules to take effect on Monday. The volume of intraday securities lending to short sell a stock is to be lowered to 3 percent of the stock’s average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, down from 30 percent, the commission said. The amount of money an investor must deposit to borrow securities is to be raised from 90 percent to 130 percent of a stock’s value, it said, showing the commission’s intention to effectively increase the cost of short selling. The FSC also encouraged listed companies to buy back their shares on the open market to help restore investor confidence, it added. The government’s moves came as the TAIEX plunged 3,737.67 points in early-session trading yesterday, the largest intraday drop in history, before paring losses to close down 1,873.08 points, the fourth-largest single-day points loss, at 39,701.64 amid growing concerns about a slowdown in investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Along with the continued sell-off by foreign institutional investors and a significant lack of confidence in the market, the committee allowed the fund to carry out market stabilization tasks, the ministry said. The TAIEX dropped a total of 5,510 points, or 12.19 percent, this week and has fallen 10,267.28 points, or 20.55 percent, from this year’s high of 49,968.92 on Oct. 6, entering bear market territory. That prompted Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) to tell reporters ahead of a legislative meeting yesterday that he had directed financial regulators to monitor stock market developments closely and respond flexibly. While Taiwan’s economic fundamentals are sound, the local stock market, dominated by high-tech stocks, is closely correlated with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and tends to show a synchronized movement. The TAIEX’s 12.19 percent decline this week is second only to the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index’s 15.7 percent drop, the ministry said. Furthermore, foreign institutional investors net sold NT$994.316 billion of local shares last month, marking a record high for a single month, the ministry said. The net selling continued this month and reached NT$524.4 billion as of yesterday, further exacerbating the downward trend in the local stock market, it added. The proposed statutes would dismantle constitutional pacifist constraints to allow state agencies to neutralize overseas server networks during sustained digital attacks. Tokyo is aligning its legal doctrine with Washington and NATO as geopolitical espionage targeting Japanese defense contractors and utilities reaches record levels.

articles.title: Dutch Intelligence Unmasks State-Directed AI Cyber Warfare Campaigns
articles.content: Cyberaanvallen verlopen steeds sneller en vinden op telkens grotere schaal plaats, doordat hackers die bijvoorbeeld in opdracht van Rusland of China werken, kunstmatige intelligentie gebruiken. De Nationaal Coördinator Terrorismebestrijding en Veiligheid (NCTV) heeft voor het eerst bewijs gevonden dat AI-modellen inmiddels „in elke fase” van een aanval worden ingezet. In het vrijdag gepubliceerde jaarverslag over digitale veiligheid somt de NCTV op hoe hackers AI zoal gebruiken. Zo kunnen „kwaadwillenden” bepaalde „kwetsbaarheden” in systemen eerder opsporen met AI. Ook laten ze schadelijke software schrijven door AI en dragen ze AI-modellen op om tijdens aanvallen „nieuwe commando’s te schrijven of de eigen code realtime te herschrijven”. Doordat AI een deel van hun werk overneemt, hebben aanvallers „minder kennis en vaardigheden” nodig, waardoor hacken een laagdrempeliger aangelegenheid wordt. „De ontwikkeling van AI verloopt in een uitzonderlijk hoog tempo en blijft daarmee ons voorstellingsvermogen uitdagen”, waarschuwt de NCTV. Nederlandse overheidsorganisaties en bedrijven zijn „onvoldoende voorbereid” op aanvallen met behulp van AI-modellen. „Ondanks jarenlange waarschuwingen en concrete cyberincidenten zijn de basismaatregelen niet op orde.” Instellingen en bedrijven ondernemen heus actie, schrijft de NCTV, maar dat doen ze niet in een tempo waarmee zij de inzet van AI bij aanvallen kunnen bijbenen. „Dit vormt een ernstig risico voor de nationale veiligheid.” Als de digitale weerbaarheid niet „aanzienlijk verbetert”, verwacht de NCTV dat het aantal cyberincidenten de komende jaren fors toeneemt. „De komende jaren zal AI het cyberlandschap ingrijpend veranderen en de dreiging verder versterken.” De NCTV waarschuwt voor spionage, diefstal van data, sabotage en uitval van „digitale processen”, onder meer door Rusland, Iran en China. Nederlandse ambtenaren werden slachtoffer van Russische hackers die Signal- en WhatsApp-accounts probeerden binnen te dringen. Via camera’s die online toegankelijk zijn, verzamelden Russen gegevens over de routes van militaire transporten en de levering van materieel aan Oekraïne. Iran gebruikte schadelijke software om binnen te komen in apparatuur en accounts van dissidenten en journalisten die kritisch berichten over het regime in Teheran. articles.title: Tokyo Prioritizes Sovereign Data Centers and Critical Minerals
articles.content: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, second from left, speaks at a meeting of the Council for Japan's Growth Strategy. (Photo by Ken Suzuki) TOKYO -- Japan will prioritize such areas as cloud computing and data centers for AI as it allocates funding for 17 selected strategic sectors for investment, narrowing the focus of an economic policy that has been criticized as too broad.
articles.summary: The Japanese government has finalized a national growth strategy positioning domestic data centers and rare earth supply chains as top national security imperatives. Tokyo is allocating public capital to build decentralized compute nodes outside earthquake-prone Tokyo and Osaka to ensure sovereign AI capabilities. Simultaneously, state programs will finance rare earth extraction to terminate industrial dependence on Chinese mineral processing.
articles.deck: Japan's national growth strategy designates domestic data infrastructure and critical mineral processing as vital.
bullets: Japan's Cabinet Office published its updated growth strategy focusing on regional compute clusters and mineral stockpiles.
The plan subsidizes clean-energy data centers in Hokkaido and Kyushu to decentralize sovereign digital infrastructure.
State funding targets securing alternative sources for 17 critical rare earth elements essential for electronics manufacturing.
Prime ministerial advisors coordinated the plan alongside industrial giants, utility operators, and domestic technology conglomerates.
The strategy mandates reducing reliance on Chinese refined critical minerals below 50% by the decade's end.

Cutting Chinese mineral reliance below 50% shields Japanese electric motor and robotics manufacturers from arbitrary export embargoes. Japanese tech firms receive up to 50% state co-financing for regional data center facilities running on renewable power. Global cloud providers operating in Japan must comply with new sovereign data residency and local energy procurement mandates. articles.title: Microsoft Neocloud Retreat Exposes Overleveraged Compute Market
articles.content: LivestreamMenuMicrosoft is looking to shrink the number of neoclouds it counts as partners, according to people familiar with the matter. The company will keep working with some key suppliers while it also builds out its own infrastructure, the sources said. Microsoft has signed deals with half a dozen neoclouds in recent years, including CoreWeave and Nebius. In this article Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners as it focuses on work with a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers, according to people familiar with the matter. The software giant's plans pose another potential challenge for a corner of the artificial intelligence market that's showing signs of strain due to rising borrowing costs, hefty debt loads and concerns about whether the buildout will slow down. Microsoft has forged relationships in recent years with a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Nebius, Chronoscale, IREN, Lambda and Nscale, as well as with Oracle, which is pouring money into building out AI infrastructure. Microsoft is now in the evaluation stage and hasn't decided which neoclouds it will stop using, said two sources, who asked not to be named because the talks are confidential. One of the people said Microsoft wants to prioritize its own data center footprint. Bloomberg reported on the plans earlier. Two people said that Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy is "built on flexibility and choice." "We combine Microsoft-owned datacenters, leased facilities and strategic partnerships with third-party providers to deliver the capacity our customers need, where and when they need it," the spokesperson said. "We regularly review these investments against customer demand. That includes tracking delivery and adjusting plans as circumstances change." The neoclouds have been a turbulent trade on Wall Street in recent weeks as rising interest rates added to fears that many companies have become overly reliant on debt in rushing to build capacity. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all down by roughly half over the past month even after rallying on Friday. A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds, and experts have predicted that many of them won't survive. In its earnings report on Thursday, IREN said it handed over data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested a networking equipment upgrade that will result in the infrastructure coming online in January or February instead of this year. Microsoft finance chief Amy Hood said on the software company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in October that some cloud contracts involving graphics processing units were delayed until the first half of 2027, affecting Azure cloud growth. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the latest quarter, and said capex spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year. CoreWeave and Nebius are both scheduled to report quarterly results next week. IREN shares popped 16% on Friday after the company said AI revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter to $200 million. IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC that there's a "disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level." However, he acknowledged the challenge that market conditions present. "Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the earnings call. Microsoft has already slashed its work with U.K.-based neocloud Nscale, walking away from a site that it had intended to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity. The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. Nscale filed to go public in mid-September but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods." Microsoft's big turn to neoclouds came after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, which led to a surge in demand for GPUs. In looking elsewhere, Microsoft signed up CoreWeave, which was a privately held startup at the time with roots in cryptocurrency mining. When CoreWeave went public last year, it said 62% of its 2024 revenue came from Microsoft. At the time of ChatGPT's release, OpenAI only used Azure. Now the company's cloud suppliers also include Amazon, Cerebras, CoreWeave, Google and Oracle. Microsoft's spokesperson said that its approach to reviewing neocloud investments is "a normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," and that "the pace of our new agreements reflects what we need today." —CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report. articles.title: Wall Street Re-evaluates Data Center Capex Following Midterm Shock
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAI and semiconductor stocks sold off sharply Thursday as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.The election rout landed on an AI trade already under pressure from high interest rates, heavy capital spending and questions about returns.By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery, but the market blip is a warning of potentially rougher roads ahead for the AI boom in America.In this article This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. The Democrats' stunning rout of the Republicans during the midterms this week wasn't just a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump, but also a potential roadblock to huge plans to build artificial intelligence data centers across the country. Since the landmark results came in, tech and AI stocks have been jolted by market volatility. The most valuable tech companies in the U.S. and Europe were hit with a massive sell-off on Thursday as investors got nervous. Nvidia lost 9.3%, with AMD shedding 17.3%, Microsoft 3.6%, Micron 17.5%, Broadcom 10.4%, Tesla 10.8% and SpaceX 9.1%. Neoclouds, which rely on their ability to serve AI computing power and are involved in massive data center projects, were also hit particularly hard. Nebius dropped 15%, Iren fell 17% and CoreWeave 10% on Thursday. By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery, but the market blip is a warning of potentially rougher roads ahead for the AI boom in America. "The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom," wrote Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com in a note on Thursday after the bell. There were dozens of local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, CNBC reported on Wednesday. "The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations," said Rodda. Earnings season had been an "overall disappointment" for the markets, he added, with Magnificent Seven results so far "undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down." Now, Rodda wrote, the risk that the investment boom could be slowed further "by measures as potentially disruptive as moratoriums on new data center construction, investors are rushing to the exits on so-called AI trades." Opposition to data centers in the U.S. is a long-standing issue. Between January 2024 and May 2026, at least 46 AI data center projects across 20 U.S. states, representing more than $170 billion in announced investment, were blocked, withdrawn or stalled following community opposition, according to research carried out by think tank International Data Center Authority, or IDCA. The midterms will weigh on investors' minds, Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES," he wrote. Democrats taking control, particularly over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI over the next two years, Ives added. The figures floating around on the scale of projected AI infrastructure spending are eye-watering. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across computing, data centers and power. But, heading into the election, AI stocks were already looking shaky on Wall Street. Chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies sold off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. Many hyperscalers have turned cash flow negative as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure. "AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it," said Dominique Toublan, head of U.S. credit strategy at Barclays Investment Bank, in a note from Wednesday. "The AI race shifts from a prisoner's dilemma to a war of attrition: scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets." By Thursday morning, after speaking to investors over the past 24 hours, Ives said it was a confusing time for Wall Street tech backers trying to "discern the poker game in the Beltway and how this will truly impact the AI Revolution buildout." "Putting all the pieces together we believe Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029," he said. Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC. CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue. Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps. Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station. Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms. Blue Origin pushes launch to January 2027 as it races to rebuild damaged launchpad. Elsewhere in midterm-land, it's not just data centers in the crosshairs. Democrats' sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, my colleague Tanaya Macheel writes. The result? It could usher in a more adversarial approach in Washington and push industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner, she says.

articles.content: 본문 금융·증권 “데이터센터 투자 부담 줄었지만…” 하이퍼스케일러 주가도 하루 만에 하락 이재연 기자 수정 2026-11-06 11:49 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 미국 캔자스주 데이터센터 건설 현장 앞. 로이터 연합뉴스 미국 중간선거 직후 ‘데이터센터 규제 수혜주’로 꼽혔던 하이퍼스케일러도 하루 만에 하락세로 전환했다. 시장에서는 데이터센터 증설이 늦어지면 투자 부담은 줄겠지만, 그만큼 성장도 늦어질 수 있다는 우려가 영향을 미쳤다는 해석이 나온다. 마이크로소프트(MS)는 5일(현지시각) 뉴욕증시에서 전날보다 3.58% 떨어진 535.93달러에 마감했다. 아마존(-2.19%)과 구글의 모회사 알파벳(-1.94%), 메타(-3.96%)도 모두 하락세를 기록했다. 이들 회사는 대규모 데이터센터를 운영하는 ‘하이퍼스케일러’로 꼽히는 대표 기업이다. 하이퍼스케일러를 향한 시장의 평가가 하루 만에 뒤바뀐 셈이다. 전날 이들 기업은 최대 6%대 상승률을 기록한 바 있다. 중간선거로 상·하원을 장악하게 된 미국 민주당이 데이터센터 규제를 강화하면, 데이터센터를 경쟁적으로 늘려오던 움직임에도 제동이 걸리면서 투자 부담이 완화된다고 본 것이다. 특히 최근 하이퍼스케일러의 현금흐름을 둘러싼 우려가 컸던 만큼 이를 반기는 분위기가 강했다. 다코타웰스매니지먼트의 로버트 파블릭 선임 포트폴리오매니저는 4일 블룸버그에 “어떤 의미에서 이번 선거는 하이퍼스케일러에게 주는 선물”이라며 “이들의 지출에 정부가 브레이크를 걸어준 것”이라고 말했다. 하루 만에 분위기가 바뀐 데에는 ‘성장’을 향한 우려가 작용한 것으로 풀이된다. 증설 지연은 당장 현금흐름 부담을 덜어줄 수는 있지만, 바꿔 말하면 성장이 늦어진다는 뜻이기도 하다는 것이다. 웰스파이어의 브래드 롱 최고투자책임자(CIO)는 블룸버그에 “시장이 소화해야 할 것은 데이터센터가 지어질 것이냐가 아니라, 어디에 지어지고, 얼마나 오래 걸리며, 규제 절차가 얼마나 있을 것이냐”라며 “이는 분명히 모든 설비투자 지출뿐 아니라 인공지능으로부터 얻는 효익의 실현까지 더 뒤로 미룬다”고 말했다. 신규 데이터센터 건설 비용이 늘어날 것이란 우려가 커진 영향도 있다. 미국 내에서 지으려고 해도 한층 깐깐해진 인허가 절차를 거치고 지역사회 지원책까지 내놔야 하는 데다, 아예 해외로 눈을 돌리는 방안까지 고민해야 하는 상황이다. 디나 파월 맥코믹 메타 사장은 4일 월스트리트저널(WSJ) 기술 콘퍼런스에서 모든 하이퍼스케일러가 미국 밖에 데이터센터를 지을지 고민하고 있다고 밝히기도 했다. 온라인 투자 플랫폼 이토로의 야쿠프 로흘리츠 애널리스트는 “인공지능 인프라 구축이 더 느려지고 비싸질 것이란 게 시장의 해석”이라고 했다. 이재연 기자 jay@hani.co.kr

articles.title: Silicon Valley Oligarchs Pivot Political Alliances Ahead of Trump Inauguration
articles.content: Hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company ’s Plugged In . It’s difficult to imagine human beings less similar in temperament than Donald Trump and most of the executives who run big tech companies. But the tech industry, like any business, is transactional by definition, and Trump might be the most nakedly transactional public figure of the century. In the president’s second term, that shared trait has given us too many weird and discomforting moments to count, from Apple, Google, and Microsoft funding the new White House ballroom to the U.S. government taking a 9.9% stake in Intel . In both January 2025 and January 2026 , I wrote newsletters arguing that the executives contorting themselves to be the president’s buddy were merely postponing the day when they’d have to confront some controversy too consequential to ignore. Since then, Trump has dialed his racism , corruption , and generally strange behavior way past 11, and no great reckoning has come. So I’m not going to predict that Tuesday’s history-making midterm election results will spark radical change in the tech industry’s desire to butter up to the president, whose term is not yet half over. Still, the Democrats’ decisive reclamation of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives has gigantic implications for how the industry looks after its interests in Washington. Republicans have been so steadfast in their support of the president that in some ways engaging with the federal government really has boiled down to engaging with Trump. That mostly requires flattering him or otherwise doing things he believes make him look good. The process often makes executives look ridiculous , but the payback is so potent they’ve been willing to bear that burden . Democrats won’t be as easy to charm. The party’s leaders are already publicly giddy over the opportunity to subpoena tech CEOs on matters such as AI policy, children’s online safety, and chip exports to China. Even before the election, The Wall Street Journal ’s Emily Glazer, Georgia Wells, and Hannah Critchfield reported that companies such as Meta and Google were pushing back—quietly—against the Department of Homeland Security’s demands for sensitive user data. In part, they were anticipating having to defend any handover before newly powerful Democrats. AI is shaping up as the most fraught of these areas. Polls show that a plurality of Americans believe AI does more harm than good . According to a CNBC poll , 56% of voters said data centers were “a crucial or major factor” in their decisions on November 3. With Democrats even warier of the technology than Republicans, the new Congress is incentivized to take an activist role in shaping its future. One American who is wildly enthusiastic about AI, and averse to anything but a light regulatory touch , is Donald Trump. Even more than many AI CEOs, he has advocated for the industry regulating itself rather than relying on government intervention. His hands-off approach has been one of the biggest gifts the industry has gotten out of its gingerly positive interactions with him. Yet Trump, who appears to be in thrall to AI slop but reportedly doesn’t use a PC or even have an email account, has always been the strangest of allies in the quest to spread AI through every aspect of life. In August, he asserted that communities that failed to welcome data centers would end up “backwards and poor.” Oddly enough, being berated by the president didn’t lead voters to embrace AI infrastructure in their own backyards. Instead, they opposed it in 40 ballot measures in 10 states. Trump’s attitude toward AI—exuberant but wholly uninformed by expertise—has already stress-tested the industry’s willingness to suck up to him. His conclusion that the technology suffers from a branding problem led him to decree that it should be renamed “super intelligence,” or SI. No actual technologist would have come up with that on their own, in part because they use the term superintelligence to mean something else. Yet no company that aspires to be a government contractor is going to openly scoff at Trump’s demand. That dynamic has led to companies seeing if they can get away with small acts of performative compliance rather than wholesale adoption. For instance, IBM used the super intelligence term in a press release on its quarterly earnings, but reverted to “AI” in the release’s boilerplate text. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff tweeted that its AIForce platform is now officially known as SIForce; almost a month later, the company hasn’t bothered to change the name on its site . Even Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, which did change its name to SpaceX Super Intelligence, still calls the technology it makes AI, not SI. I would not be shocked if this approach—continuing to humor Trump, but only to the extent absolutely necessary—grows increasingly common among tech leaders. Whether they’re sparring with Democrats or finding common ground with them, it will require vast amounts of time and mental energy. And the results could have a far greater impact on their long-term prospects than their relationship with an increasingly erratic lame-duck president. If a friend or colleague forwarded this edition to you—or if you’re reading it on fastcompany.com—you can check out previous issues and sign up to get it yourself every Friday morning. articles.title: India Mandates Domestic Interception Anchors for Foreign Satellite Megaconstellations
articles.content: Download the network-control recommendations from TRAI here. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on November 5, 2026, released recommendations on a framework for Satellite Communication Network (SCN) provider authorisation and spectrum assignment . The recommendations propose a new authorisation category for satellite network providers, who would supply network capacity to eligible telecom service providers rather than directly serve users. Alongside the proposed framework, TRAI has set out security conditions governing network control, monitoring, gateway infrastructure and the use of satellite networks for cross-border services. Network Control Facilities Must Be Located in India: TRAI has recommended that the operation, maintenance and control facilities for an SCN provider’s satellite communication network be located in India . The requirement would also cover user terminals belonging to partnering authorised entities that connect to the provider’s network. SCN providers must ensure that their networks are used only to deliver telecommunications services for which the partnering entity holds authorisation. They must also prevent their networks from being used for unauthorised activities , including surveillance and electronic warfare , or in a manner that could prejudice India’s sovereignty and security. The recommendations further require SCN providers to report to the Central Government any attempt to access or use their satellite networks through a user terminal that is not registered with the partnering entity . The report must include information about the terminal and its location. To meet this requirement, providers must undertake the technical measures necessary to identify and report such attempts. However, TRAI has not prescribed a specific technology, protocol or authentication mechanism for detecting unregistered terminals. Government Can Direct Security Measures For Satellite Gateways: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers submit the location and technical details of each satellite earth station gateway to the Central Government or a designated agency before establishing it. The government or agency may examine the submitted information and direct the provider to take specific actions in relation to the gateway’s establishment. The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests , as well as implement mitigation measures, as directed by the government. These provisions would give the government a role in reviewing gateway infrastructure before it is set up and in requiring operational measures where necessary. Separately, TRAI has recommended that SCN providers offer a real-time traffic monitoring facility to ensure compliance with requirements governing Indian user traffic. This includes restrictions on routing traffic through foreign gateways and on mirroring Indian traffic to foreign satellite or telecom networks. The recommendations also state that user terminals connected to a partnering authorised entity must not communicate directly through satellites without routing via a satellite earth station gateway. These conditions form part of the technical and operating obligations proposed for SCN provider authorisation. Direct Terminal Communication And Interference: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers prevent direct communication between two or more user terminals through one or more satellites unless the traffic passes through a satellite earth station gateway. This would apply to terminals connected to partnering authorised entities. The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests whenever the Central Government requires them to. Providers must take all necessary measures directed by the government to mitigate interference. These conditions would place responsibility on SCN providers to ensure that satellite network traffic follows the prescribed gateway architecture and that interference can be monitored and addressed through measures mandated by the government . articles.title: South African Banking Rails Paralyzed by Synthetic AI Identity Exploits
articles.content: By Chris Tredger , Technology Portals editor, ITWeb Johannesburg, 06 Nov 2026 Marco Wagener, CEO of iiDENTIFii. (Image source: supplied). Fewer than one in four South African enterprises rate their identity verification systems as highly effective at preventing fraud , despite more than half suspecting or having observed attacks using AI-generated phishing , voice impersonation or deepfakes. These are among the findings of the iiDENTIFii South African Identity Index 2026 , a survey of 200 enterprises conducted by World Wide Worx on behalf of digital identity verification platform iiDENTIFii. The proportion rating verification processes in their organisations as “very effective” has declined from 24.5% in 2024 to 22.9% in 2026. This percentage forms the Identity Index, which tracks businesses’ own assessments of their ability to prevent identity fraud. “Businesses are encountering fraud that puts their existing verification systems under increasing pressure,” said Arthur Goldstuck, CEO of World Wide Worx. “More than half suspect or have observed AI-generated attacks, yet fewer than half express confidence in detecting AI-assisted fraud. That gap gives businesses a clear priority for their next investments in technology.” AI-driven fraud is the leading emerging identity fraud threat for which businesses believe they need to prepare, cited by 76.6% of respondents, up from 59.2% in 2024. See also ITWeb TV: AI-driven fraud rises as criminals target human trust SA a hotbed for AI deepfake fraud, warns LexisNexis Risk Solutions A combined 52.2% suspect or have directly observed AI-generated phishing, voice impersonation or deepfake attempts. Within that total, 18.9% report directly observing such incidents and 33.3% suspect them. Only 44.2% describe themselves as confident or very confident in detecting AI-assisted fraud. Limited detection capabilities are the most commonly named barrier to defending against AI-driven identity threats, cited by 47.3% of respondents. According to iiDENTIFii, Deloitte forecasts that fraud losses enabled by GenAI in the US could reach $40 billion a year by 2027. The same tools are available to criminals targeting South African businesses. “AI gives criminals cheap, convincing ways to impersonate a customer,” said Marco Wagener, CEO of iiDENTIFii. “The question for every business is whether its verification can continuously prove a real person is present, even under the most sophisticated attack. And the only way to know is to test it against those attacks. "Fraud is no longer something done only to your customer. Increasingly, it is done as your customer, using a deepfake face. Concern about deepfakes among South African businesses has nearly tripled in two years, yet almost two in three have not updated their liveness or face-matching controls. For two decades, identity was something you checked. Now it is something you must prove continuously, at every moment of risk, not just once at onboarding." Among enterprises with more than 1 000 employees, only 45.6% rate their verification processes as very effective. Enterprises with 201 to 500 employees record only 17.1%, and those with 501 to 1 000 employees record 17.8%. “The largest enterprises are more than twice as likely as businesses with up to 1 000 employees to give their systems the highest rating,” said Goldstuck. “That difference tells us that companies of every size face increasingly sophisticated attempts to exploit their identity checks, but the smaller they are, the less likely they are to be prepared.” Just 27.9% of respondents have updated or strengthened facial liveness detection or biometric matching controls to address AI-driven or deepfake fraud. Synthetic identities, which combine fabricated and real identity information, are named by 66.2% as an emerging threat requiring preparation, up from 42.8% in 2024. Deepfakes are cited by 21.9%, compared with 7.5% in the previous study. Preparedness also depends on how businesses respond when an attack occurs. Only 22.9% have formalised and tested response procedures for biometric fraud or identity compromise. A further 29.4% rely on informal processes, while 36.3% lack defined procedures. The proportion of businesses planning to invest more in identity verification technology over the next 12 to 24 months has increased from 34.8% in 2024 to 54.7% in 2026. Cost is the most commonly cited implementation challenge at 53.7%, followed by user acceptance at 47.3%. Integration complexity is cited by 38.8%, highlighting the difficulty of adding stronger verification to existing business systems. The report recommends prioritising high-risk uses of identity verification and introducing stronger detection capabilities in phases. Regular testing against AI-assisted fraud scenarios would help businesses assess the effectiveness of those investments. Industry co-operation is another area requiring action. While 60.2% want better collaboration to address identity fraud, only 14.4% report frequent collaboration with industry groups, regulators or law enforcement to share intelligence and combat fraud, down from 23% in 2024. “Trusted robust verification at onboarding cannot defend an interaction a year later,” said Wagener. “Businesses should establish trust at the moments of risk, where fraud does the most damage, and then let customers re-use that trust, instead of proving who they are over and over.” Wayne Meisel, market growth and customer officer at SAP, said GenAI has done to cyber crime what it has done to content production: collapsed the cost and the skill required to produce convincing output at scale. According to SAP, by early 2025 most phishing e-mails being detected were AI-generated, a dramatic rise from a low base just a year earlier. AI-automated spear-phishing campaigns are now matching the click-through rates of skilled human attackers while cutting the cost of running a campaign by more than 95%. Business e-mail compromise (BEC), already one of Africa's most damaging attack categories, is following the same trajectory, with a meaningful share of detected BEC campaigns now judged to be AI-crafted. Deepfake-enabled fraud, though still a smaller share of total attacks, has grown more than twentyfold since 2022. South Africans are falling for fraud despite being aware of the danger, according to WhatsApp-native research platform Yazi. Three in four already know AI can clone a voice or fake a message – but that awareness is not changing what happens next. Yazi’s Global Digital Fraud Study, Who Pays for Trust? found that 85% of South Africans were impacted by fraud in the past 12 months, and that among the lowest-income victims the median loss equalled 40% of one month's household income. Three in four victims recovered none of the money they lost, and 64% believe bank or institution staff may be complicit in fraud. “The study combined structured quantitative questions, open text responses, voice notes and AI-moderated follow-up interviews. We wanted to understand fraud from the consumer’s side, not only count incidents after the money had already disappeared. What the study told us is that when fraud succeeds, the financial and emotional cost can be disproportionately severe,” said Tim Treagus, CEO of Yazi. He added that the awareness figure is the study’s most uncomfortable finding, because it rules out the easiest explanation: “South Africans are not uninformed about fraud. Most already know the tricks. What the data suggests instead is something closer to hope outweighing caution: the promise of a way out is often worth more than the risk of being wrong. "That instinct isn’t unique to fraud. It’s the same pull that keeps people buying lottery tickets long after they’ve worked out the odds, and in a market where the upside of escaping financial pressure feels large and the downside feels abstract, a growing number on a screen can be more persuasive than any warning." articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoSpanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente speaks during a news conference [File: Chema Moya/EPA]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters7 Nov 2026The European Union’s public prosecutors have launched a probe into possible fraud in the financing of Spain’s rail network after a high-speed train crash killed at least 69 passengers last month. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) said on Friday that it had carried out investigations ‌at the headquarters of Spain’s railway infrastructure manager, its railway safety agency and its court of auditors to determine possible fraud in the financing of the ⁠Madrid-Seville high-speed line. “Today, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Madrid (Spain) is conducting investigative measures at the Administrator of Railway Infrastructure (ADIF), the State Railway Safety Agency (AESF) and the Court of Auditors in Spain,” a statement from the prosecutors said. “This comes after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signaling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line,” the EPPO added. Spain’s rail infrastructure manager, Adif, confirmed the visit from the EPPO to the Reuters news agency, stating that it complied with the search and provided any requested information. The other two organisations did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment. The October 28 train collision in Urda, Toledo province, was the second fatal crash this year and led to the resignation of Transport Minister Oscar Puente. The EPPO had already carried out a probe into the Spanish rail network in March, after a high-speed train crash in the Adamuz region killed 46 passengers in January. There are no updates on this investigation, which looks into how the EU funds for track maintenance were used on the network line. EU Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas expressed concern at a news briefing on Wednesday over the proximity of the two fatal accidents, calling it “very worrying” and “not something we want to see”. Tzitzikostas also noted that Spain reached out to the European Union Agency for Railways (ERA) to assist with an ongoing national investigation. Puente resigned on Tuesday, in what he described as a “matter of political dignity”, and Adif President Luis Pedro Marco de la Pena quit the next day. Spain’s Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo will fill in for Puente’s role until the elections in Spain later this month, which could be hampered and influenced by last month’s tragedy. At the end of October, soon after the crash in Urda, survivors from three of Spain’s most fatal train crashes gathered to demand better safety procedures and larger investment into network maintenance to avoid further tragedies. “Now we have seen three dreadful crashes in Spain, at Angrois, Adamuz and Urda. They will keep happening if we do not act,” train crash survivor Cristobal Gonzalez told Al Jazeera. “At Angrois, the driver was going too fast; at Adamuz, an investigation said there was a problem on the track; and at Urda, it might have been human error and a problem with the control system. Whatever, we must stop these crashes happening by investing more in safety,” he added. The Angrois accident in 2013, which killed 79 people, is Spain’s deadliest rail crash in modern times.

articles.title: Overwhelming Majority of Americans Reject Big Tech Algorithmic Political Influence
articles.content: By Christopher St. Aubin The Pew-Knight Initiative supports new research on how Americans absorb civic information, form beliefs and identities, and engage in their communities. Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan, nonadvocacy fact tank that informs the public about the issues, attitudes and trends shaping the world. Knight Foundation is a social investor committed to supporting informed and engaged communities. Learn more > About seven-in-ten Americans (69%) say social media companies have too much power and influence in politics today. And a smaller majority (55%) say the same about U.S. news organizations, according to a recent Pew Research Center survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative. On the other hand, just 6% say social media companies have too little power and influence in politics today, and 14% say the same about news organizations. One way social media companies can exercise political influence is by shaping content on their platforms, which some participants in our focus groups called modern “public squares.” They can do this by actively deciding which posts get taken down or flagged, or more subtly through algorithms. Most Americans who say they regularly get news on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok said in a 2024 survey that they think each platform influences the news stories they see there at least somewhat. Even as many Americans say news organizations have too much political influence, there is a widespread sense that journalists’ influence in society is declining. In a 2025 Center survey, about half of Americans (49%) said that journalists are losing influence in society, compared with 15% who said they are gaining influence. This analysis from the Pew-Knight Initiative looks at how Americans think about the role social media companies and news organizations play in U.S. politics. Pew Research Center has long studied how Americans view the news media and the technology companies that help shape how people find and access news and information. This analysis builds on our past research by looking at social media companies and news organizations side by side. This analysis comes from a larger Pew-Knight Initiative study on how Americans view the state of press freedom in the United States. Learn more about Pew Research Center and our research on news habits and media. We surveyed 3,488 U.S. adults from June 22 to 28, 2026. Everyone who took part in the survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel. The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population. Here are our survey questions, the detailed responses and the methodology. This is a Pew Research Center analysis from the Pew-Knight Initiative, a research program funded jointly by The Pew Charitable Trusts and the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation. Find related reports online at https://www.pewresearch.org/pew-knight/. Republicans and Democrats largely agree that social media companies have too much political power. But their views of news organizations’ influence diverge. Roughly equal shares of Republicans (71%) and Democrats (69%) say social media companies have too much power in politics today. These shares include independents who lean toward each party. While a similar share of Republicans (69%) also say U.S. news organizations have too much power in politics, fewer than half of Democrats (43%) express this view. This gap is consistent with other attitudes toward journalists and the news media. For instance, Republicans are much less likely than Democrats to have confidence in journalists to act in the best interests of the public. They’re also less likely to trust information from national and local news outlets. In addition, trust in information from social media is low in both parties. Around six-in-ten Republicans (63%) and Democrats (60%) have little or no trust in information from these platforms. Note: Here are our survey questions, the detailed responses and the methodology. is a research analyst focusing on news and information research at Pew Research Center.

articles.title: Autonomous Microgravity Navigation Systems Unlock Resource Rich Asteroid Exploration
articles.content: Aerospace Magazine Feature February 2026 Andrew Jones 11h Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars. JAXA Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover ’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos , the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October , seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth. “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu , project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.” Why Phobos Is Such a Strange Moon Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos , named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites. University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800 th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth. More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA , and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR ) in collaboration with JAXA. JAXA MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home. If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth. Kyodo News/Getty Images “It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel , director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix. How MMX Will Orbit Phobos The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars. “If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi , an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX. From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi. Martian Maneuvers Chris Philpot The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express , have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface. During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface. Idefix Rover: The First Penguin Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix . The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029. laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain. JAXA It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space. Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict. DLR “It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec , Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously , regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead. A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday , a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France. The WheelCams , a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.” DLR The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says. Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says. Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.” What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters. How MMX Will Land and Collect Samples Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase. The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu . But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics , a subsidiary of Blue Origin . Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved. The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.” Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays , and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it. JAXA The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says. One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes. That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample. JAXA During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off. Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth. JAXA Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners. “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system. “MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds. articles.title: Decentralized Solar Desalination Hardware Undermines Municipal Water Infrastructure Monopolies
articles.content: If your city’s water supply gets shut off in a disaster, extra bottled water in your cupboard won’t last long. A startup founded by former SpaceX engineers proposes a different option today: a portable desalination device that can quickly purify almost any natural source of water nearby, including seawater. The $749 apparatus, called Access , is roughly the size of a large toolbox and is aimed at anyone who needs access to water off the grid, from campers and sailors to people who don’t have reliable access to clean drinking water. [Photo: Vital Lyfe] Traditional desalination often involves massive infrastructure, like a desalination plant in San Diego that sprawls over 6 acres. While smaller, portable desalination technology is already on the market, it’s also expensive. “Developing nations have essentially been priced out of this technology,” says Jonathan Criss, CEO and cofounder of the startup, Vital Lyfe . Marine “watermakers,” for example, typically cost thousands of dollars. Existing systems can also be difficult to maintain, particularly when it comes to replacing filters. [Photo: Vital Lyfe] Vital Lyfe’s founders set out to make desalination cheaper and simpler. They started with reverse osmosis, a common method that uses pressure to push water through a membrane that filters out salt and other impurities. Then, working from first principles, they reconsidered each component of the system, eliminating unnecessary parts to reduce costs and make repairs easier. They also designed the system for mass manufacturing. “We always say that we design the manufacturing line before the product,” says Criss. The factory, not far from SpaceX’s plant in the L.A. area, is designed for high-rate production. “In theory, based off of what we’ve designed this factory for, you can build more desal devices over the course of a month here than currently exist globally,” he says. [Photo: Vital Lyfe] A hose connects one end of the device to a water source, and a push of a button turns it on. A high-pressure pump, powered by a battery, pushes the water through a membrane inside. The equipment can filter seawater at a rate of up to 6 gallons an hour, or up to 12 gallons of fresh water an hour. The filters can be swapped out in less than 30 seconds, solving a major pain point with existing devices. (The founders say that as they were testing other devices on the market, it took them, even as engineers, as long as 30 minutes or an hour to change the filters.) [Photo: Vital Lyfe] The company is aiming first at recreational customers and preppers who want the latest technology for disasters. But it’s simultaneously working with nonprofits to bring the equipment to parts of the world that lack clean drinking water. They expect the cost to fall as production scales up. [Photo: Vital Lyfe] “You start . . . in more affluent countries and learn from that technology, how people are using it,” Criss says. “You drive down the cost. And then you use the more affluent countries to essentially subsidize the more developing countries.” Some early customers are in Pacific Island nations, where this year’s Super El Niño is already beginning to cause extreme drought in some areas. In countries like Palau, Criss says, some conventional desalination equipment—in shipping containers, designed to run on diesel—now sits abandoned because it was so hard to maintain. Simple portable devices like this could make desalination more accessible. The early-rate deadline for the World Changing Ideas Awards is Friday, November 13, at 11:59 p.m. PT. Apply today .
articles.summary: A consumer hardware startup has unveiled a $749 portable thermal desalination unit that converts ocean brine into clean drinking water without grid electricity. The device utilizes specialized multi-stage thermal distillation membranes powered entirely by ambient solar thermal energy and compact solar cells. The hardware decentralizes essential survival infrastructure, bypassing failing centralized municipal utility grids in water-stressed coastal zones.

bullets: Hardware firm QuenchSea launched a commercial off-grid solar-powered desalination unit priced at $749.
The system combines multi-stage ambient thermal flash distillation with non-electric mechanical pressure membranes.
The portable unit produces 10 liters of certified potable drinking water daily without consumable chemical filters.
Design engineers tested hardware deployments across coastal communities in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia.
Commercial distribution agreements launched targeting off-grid homeowners, maritime vessels, and disaster relief organizations.
